Lyubar Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Lyubar may have had a wooden synagogue as early as 1491. During the Paliy Uprising of 1702–1704, the town's Jews fled the advancing Cossacks, with only 7 returning by 1703; five Jewish families from Lyubar later settled in Medzhybizh in 1717 — a town of major significance in Hasidic history, later home to the Baal Shem Tov himself. Enough Lyubar Jews had emigrated to the US by 1895 to form their own hometown society. During the Civil War, in 1920, Red Army soldiers — a notably rare attribution in this collection, where most pogroms were carried out by other forces — staged a pogrom in Lyubar, killing about 50 and wounding over 180. Lyubar was the birthplace of Aron Vergelis (1918–99), editor-in-chief of the Soviet Yiddish journal Sovetish Heymland, one of the few officially sanctioned Yiddish publications in the USSR. The worst single day of the Holocaust here came on September 13, 1941, when 1,119 Lyubar residents and about 180 Jews from nearby communities were shot at a sandlot.
